Some modern Salafis give a different account of the attempts by the “philosophers of Islam” to reconcile religion and philosophy. Their view contradicts the model presented here by Tawfiq al-Tawil, even though al-Tawil himself also follows a Salafi approach. Mahmud Qasim, for example, argues that Ibn Rushd merely brought religion together with Aristotle’s philosophy, without intending to defend philosophy itself. His aim, Qasim says, was to defend religion, as shown by the fact that he modified Aristotle’s philosophy and accepted from it only what he believed to be true. See Mahmud Qasim, Ibn Rushd, the Misrepresented Philosopher, Cairo, Anglo-Egyptian Bookshop, pp. 45–46. This disagreement among Salafis over how to understand the attempt to “reconcile” religion and philosophy in our philosophical heritage shows that the alleged reconciliation is not an objective historical reality, but a set of subjective interpretations imposed by shared ideological starting points. Most of these interpretations are also highly selective.↩︎

The method Taha Husayn followed in On Pre-Islamic Poetry was historical in a relative sense, but not historical in the full sense of the term. He tried to identify certain historical phenomena to support his view that pre-Islamic poetry was not actually pre-Islamic but later fabrication. We disagree with his conclusions, while still seeing his method as the beginning of a revolt against the traditionalist method.↩︎

Plato says in his famous dialogue (4A 2): “The ignorant do not concern themselves with philosophy and do not want to become wise, because the ugliness of ignorance lies in this: a person who is neither beautiful, complete, nor intelligent is nevertheless completely satisfied with himself and thinks he needs nothing, and therefore does not desire what he believes he does not need.” The “ignorant” in Plato’s formulation here are neither the gods nor the philosophers; they are the slaves. The judgment that a human being is not beautiful, complete, intelligent, and so on excludes philosophers and places a fixed metaphysical barrier before the development of the lower classes and before any possibility that they might reach the level of philosophy. Their ignorance is therefore treated as innate and unchangeable.↩︎

This railway was built before the First World War under an agreement between the Ottoman Turkish government and Imperial Germany. Germany was among the imperial powers most eager to control this important part of the Arab region and the strategic route to the Gulf, which opened onto seas and oceans of great strategic importance. The Iraqi national movement viewed the project with suspicion and anxiety from the start. This national concern appears in some literary writing from the period. The Iraqi poet Muhammad Rida al-Shabibi, for example, wrote in 1918:↩︎

> They laid the iron rails, but our bonds were not extended by a rope; > instead, a trap was laid for us. > When railway lines intertwine, > they become a net in which the East of the land is caught. > > (*Diwan al-Shabibi*, Cairo, 1940, p. 36.)

Becker said this in a lecture to the Kaiser Wilhelm Society in Berlin in March 1931. Abd al-Rahman Badawi translated the lecture from German under the title “The Heritage of the Ancients in East and West.” He published it together with studies by other Orientalists in a single book called The Greek Heritage in Islamic Civilization, Dar al-Nahda al-Arabiyya, Cairo, 2nd ed., 1965. In introducing Becker, Badawi writes that “politics knew him (...) and scholarship knew him as an Orientalist and philosopher of civilization (...) He came from a family belonging to the bourgeois class, the class that dominated other classes throughout the nineteenth century in Europe generally, and in Germany especially from the Franco-Prussian War until the Great War, because it embodied the political, moral, and economic values dominant in that century.” Same source, p. 299. This description helps illuminate the ideological dimensions of Becker’s ideas here.↩︎
